title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. The confirmatory design used a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model: gpt-5-mini), and a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) running the full_intent_constraint_validation rule. Execution used shared-initial-candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task reused across arms) and allowed at most one bounded repair attempt per task. All planned episodes completed (planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480) with model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms: n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Two preregistration/execution issues affect interpretation: (1) shared-generation semantics removed the per-arm stochasticity assumed by the preregistered power calculation, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR provided no additional verifier-detectable benefit in this executed artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred; results do not generalize beyond the executed semantics, model, task bank, repair budget, or verifier.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) offer promising productivity gains for network operators by converting natural-language intent into device configurations, but stochastic generation can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate operational invariants (reachability, workflow ordering, protected interfaces). Deterministic validators and iterative repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) are widely proposed to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects before deployment. To provide an artifact-backed, preregistered assessment of bounded GVR in a controlled setting, we executed a confirmatory paired experiment (study c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) comparing an unconstrained generator baseline to a guarded GVR arm on a public synthetic NetOps task bank (240 paired tasks). The run used a single generator/prompt pairing (requested model: gpt-5-mini), a pybatfish-style deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applying a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set, and a bounded repair budget of one LLM-guided repair attempt per task. The execution adhered to preregistered analysis logic (paired_binary_analysis_v1) but used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one initial generated candidate per task reused for both arms), which removes per-condition stochasticity and therefore eliminates within-pair discordance potential. We report the preregistered estimand, exact confirmatory outcomes from the frozen analysis executor, and a focused interpretation constrained to what the archived execution and analyses support.
sections.related_work: Three research streams ground this study. First, empirical work documents that LLMs can hallucinate or produce incorrect outputs when generating code or structured artifacts, motivating deterministic verification in production pipelines (e.g., surveys and empirical studies summarized in the literature) and demonstrating that surface plausibility is a weak proxy for domain-level correctness. Second, method and systems research on GVR and constrained decoding shows that interposing validators and constrained generation improves mechanically checkable properties (compilation, syntactic validity, schema compliance) in many domains; these case studies provide conceptual support for GVR but also emphasize that syntactic gains do not imply semantic correctness against domain-specific invariants. Representative examples include recent work on generate-and-verify architectures and grammar/schema-constrained decoding strategies (see, e.g., NetConfEval and related NetOps evaluations [10.1145/3656296]). Third, NetOps-specific research advocates verifier-driven evaluations combining topology- and policy-aware checks with human oversight; prototype systems integrating LLMs with such verifiers report operational benefits but also emphasize residual oracle incompleteness and the need for adversarial testing. Our study differs by preregistering the estimand and analysis executor, freezing execution artifacts before outcome observation, and executing a paired confirmatory design on a synthetic task bank with deterministic verification rules while explicitly executing under shared-initial-candidate semantics.
sections.methodology: Estimand, hypotheses, and preregistered analysis. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (proportion difference of verifier-accepted tasks: rate(C) − rate(A)), computed by the frozen registered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Confirmatory hypotheses compared guarded GVR (C) against unconstrained generation (A) and, prespecified but not executed here, against schema-constrained decoding (B). The primary test was an exact two-sided McNemar test on paired binary outcomes; absolute risk differences and paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals were also computed (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Design and execution. The experiment used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter_family and requested generator gpt-5-mini. Important executed parameters (as recorded in the execution manifest) were generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 (one bounded repair). The deterministic validator executed a full_intent_constraint_validation rule that enforces required command sequences, topology-aware reachability, protected-interface preservation, and final-state predicates; the validator returns structured diagnostics (violation_count, violation_codes, and explicit validator traces). Task bank. The public synthetic NetOps task bank comprises 12 topology/policy clusters with 20 tasks per cluster (240 tasks total). Each task encodes an initial device state, an intent with an expected required_sequence, workflow constraints, and an expected final state. Task difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) are used by the validator to label traces and to support exploratory moderator analyses. Execution semantics and rationales. We chose a shared-initial-candidate generation semantics to reduce provider-call costs during the hosted run; this decision was preregistered in the adapter execution_contract for the executed run but departs from the independent-generation assumption used in the preregistered power calculation. The repair loop is bounded and only invoked when the deterministic validator reports a violation; repair attempts are constrained by an edit budget in the preregistration and are recorded in validator traces. Reproducibility and artifact fidelity. The preregistration, execution manifest, validator traces, and analysis outputs were frozen before observing outcomes and form the authoritative record for all numerical claims reported here.
sections.results: Execution accounting. Planned_episode_count = 480 (two conditions × 240 tasks); completed_episode_count = 480; failed_episode_count = 0; complete_pair_count = 240. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, the run consumed model_calls_used = 240 (one shared initial generation per task) rather than the maximum permitted 480. Validator-level outcomes. For every task the shared initial candidate passed the deterministic verifier: contingency counts n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate (rate_GVR − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI (percentile; 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair usage. No repair attempts were applied in any episode: repair_applied = false for all episodes and every validator trace. Degeneracy and inferential consequence. The absence of any within-pair discordant outcomes (zero discordant pairs) produces a degenerate paired comparison: the paired test and bootstrap produce a point estimate and interval of exactly zero with p = 1.00 because there is no within-pair information to estimate or reject a differential effect. This degeneracy is a direct consequence of the executed shared-generation semantics, which contradict the independent-generation assumption underlying the preregistered power calculation and thereby removes the discordance potential that GVR could exploit.
sections.discussion: Conservative interpretation. In this executed, artifact-backed regime—single generator/prompt pairing (requested gpt-5-mini), shared-initial-candidate semantics, synthetic task bank (N=240), bounded single repair attempt, and a deterministic pybatfish-style verifier—bounded GVR produced no additional verifier-detectable benefit because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. This null result is narrowly scoped: it does not imply GVR is ineffective in settings with independent per-arm generation, higher generator error rates, broader verifier coverage, larger repair budgets, or different models. Design lessons and diagnostic implications. Two evaluation choices principally determine the ability to measure GVR efficacy: (1) generation semantics (shared vs independent) sets discordance potential between arms—measuring GVR as a corrective mechanism for stochastic generator errors requires independent per-condition generation; (2) verifier completeness and adversarial task selection determine whether the task bank produces verifier-detectable failures. The preregistration included golden-reference injections (10% of tasks) and adversarial checks to validate verifier sensitivity; the archived adapter-configured run did not realize the golden-injection step, leaving an operational gap in oracle validation. Practical recommendations for robust evaluation. To restore preregistered inferential assumptions and meaningfully measure GVR: (a) rerun the task bank with independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives independent stochastic draws, (b) inject golden/adversarial tasks (as prespecified) to validate verifier sensitivity to realistic failure modes, (c) expand model coverage beyond a single generator and increase the repair budget to observe iterative repair behavior, and (d) broaden verifier invariants to reduce oracle incompleteness risk. These recommendations follow directly from the preregistered design and the observed execution accounting rather than from post hoc speculation. Representative example and diagnostics. A typical task and its recorded traces illustrate the outcome pattern: intent = "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up." The shared initial generated configuration (example preserved in the validator trace) was: "interface edge1 admin down; interface edge1 vlan 30; interface edge1 mtu 1600; interface edge1 admin up"; the deterministic validator recorded violation_count = 0 both before and after (validation_before.violation_count = 0; validation_after.violation_count = 0) and repair_applied = false. Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared-generation semantics violated the preregistered independent-generation power assumption and eliminated discordance potential. Construct validity: passing the deterministic validator does not guarantee absence of operational risks outside the verifier’s encoded invariants (oracle incompleteness). External validity: synthetic tasks, one model (gpt-5-mini), and a single bounded repair iteration constrain generalization. Conclusion validity: zero discordant outcomes preclude evidence that bounded GVR changes verifier-detectable rates under the executed semantics. Operational implications. For operational deployments where GVR is intended as an automatic corrective layer, evaluation must use per-condition independent generation, adversarial/golden tasks that exercise verifier failure modes, and a sufficiently rich verifier to surface domain-relevant semantic violations. Otherwise, null verifier-level outcomes (as observed here) may reflect either genuinely reliable generation or verifier blind spots, and cannot distinguish those possibilities.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment evaluating bounded GVR for intent→configuration NetOps on a public synthetic task bank. Under the executed shared-generation semantics every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier (n11 = 240), yielding a degenerate paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Conservatively interpreted, bounded GVR did not add verifier-detectable value in this artifact-backed setting because no verifier-detectable errors occurred. Two execution deviations constrain inference: (1) shared-generation semantics removed the per-arm stochasticity assumed in the preregistered power calculation, and (2) the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison was not executed in the archived run. The archived preregistration, execution manifest, validator traces, and frozen analysis executor contain the authoritative records for these claims. Future evaluations that restore independent per-arm generation, include golden/adversarial task injections, expand model and repair budgets, and broaden verifier invariant coverage are required to test whether GVR provides measurable corrective benefits in operationally realistic NetOps regimes.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore reduced sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
